Partners

ATKAYVA is a network, and the network is open. If you own a machine, a truck or a bus, lead a crew, practise engineering or supply material on this coast, and you keep your word, there may be a place in it for you.

NKovaya

Nobody entered this network on the strength of a brochure. Each partner earned a place on a live site, under deadline, with a client watching. The door is open to anyone ready to do the same.

Who we are looking for

Machinery owners

Excavators, breakers, cranes, rigs, rollers, mixers and pumps, with operators.

Transporters and fleet owners

Tippers, trailers, low-loaders and bulkers. Buses, cars and utility vehicles.

Labour contractors and crew leaders

Skilled trades and general labour, properly paid and properly papered.

Consultants and suppliers

Engineers, laboratories, material suppliers and fabricators.

How the network works

The standard

How a partner is admitted, what is checked, and how a place is kept.

Payments

How rates are agreed, how work is counted and when you are paid.

Register

Tell us what you own or what you do.

What a partner gets

Work
From a firm that is called first by the plants of this belt.
Payment as agreed
On the date promised, through the bank, against a statement you can check.
Fair counting
Hours, trips and weights recorded together and signed by both sides.
No demands
Nobody at ATKAYVA may ask you for money or a favour in return for work or payment. If anyone does, tell the leadership.
A hearing
If you disagree with a decision, the leadership of the firm will hear you.

What we ask

One thing above the rest. Do what you said you would do, and tell us at once when you cannot.

Everything else is in the partner code.

Ready to be tried on a job?

A first call is always a modest one. The second depends on the first.

What we call for

Excavators
From 5 to 50 tonnes. Heavy machines with rock breakers are in constant demand in this basalt.
Cranes
Mobile cranes up to 35 tonnes, pick-and-carry cranes and crawler cranes.
Earthmoving
Bulldozers and vibratory rollers.
Piling
Rigs for bored piles.
Concrete
Transit mixers, self-loading mixers, concrete pumps and boom pumps.

What we look for

In the machine

In the operator

In the owner

How a call works

  1. We call

    With the class of machine, the place, the start time and the likely duration.

  2. You say yes or no

    An honest no is worth more to us than a doubtful yes.

  3. Terms are confirmed in writing

    Rate, the basis of hire, working hours, fuel, operator, shifting and who pays for what. A message is enough.

  4. The machine is inspected at the gate

    By our supervisor and usually by the client’s safety team.

  5. Hours are recorded each shift

    On a log sheet signed by your operator and our supervisor.

  6. You are paid on the agreed date

    See Payments.

If your machine breaks down

Tell us at once. If you can repair it within the time the job can wait, do so, and our mechanical support team will help where it can. If you cannot, we will bring another machine from the network.

A breakdown honestly reported costs you the hours lost. A breakdown concealed costs you your place.

Emergency calls

Some of our calls come at night, for a plant that is down. Owners who answer those calls, and whose machines can move within minutes, are the heart of this network. We remember who came.

Skill that can be shown
Each tradesman is tested by us before deployment. A welder welds. A rigger rigs.
People who are fit

Adults

A network is only as strong as the standard that binds it. Ours is short, and it is applied to everyone in the same way.

NKovaya

Partners
  • Partners overview

Join the network

  • Transporters and fleet owners
  • Labour contractors
  • Consultants and suppliers

How it works

  • The standard
  • Payments
  • Register

Three things we measure

Everything else follows from these.

Reliability

Did you come when you said, with what you promised?

Safety

Did your people and machines follow the rules without being told twice?

Honesty

Did you tell us the truth, in your papers, your hours and your bad news?

Entering the network

  1. Register

    On the registration page, or by telephone.

  2. We come and look

    At the machine, the vehicle, the crew or the workshop, where it stands. Papers are checked against the thing itself.

  3. You read and accept the partner code

    See Partner code. In Gujarati, Hindi or English.

  4. A first job

    A modest one, beside people we already trust.

  5. A review

    After the first job, by the supervisor who ran it and the project manager. You are told what was found.

Keeping a place

A place in the network is held by the last job, and not by the first.

After every job the supervisor records how the partner performed on the three measures. The project managers and the leadership of the firm look at those records when deciding whom to call first.

Partners who are called first
Reliable, safe and honest, job after job. They get the emergency calls, the long contracts and our recommendation.
Partners who are called
Sound, with something to improve. We say what.
Partners who are paused
After a serious lapse. They may return when the cause has been put right.
Partners who are removed
For a bribe, a false paper, a concealed injury, underpaying workers or retaliation against someone who spoke up.

What is checked at the gate

For We check
Machines Papers, operator’s licence, condition, safety devices, leaks. For cranes, load chart and test certificates.
Vehicles Papers, driver’s licence, tyres, brakes, lights, reverse alarm, tarpaulin, extinguisher.
People Identity, age, medical fitness, skill, induction.
Materials Source, delivery papers, weight, test certificate, visual condition.
Tools and tackle Inspection tags, test certificates, guards, cables.

A machine, vehicle or person that fails is turned back. It is not an insult. It is the standard.

Fairness

  • The standard is the same for a relative of the leadership of the firm as for a stranger. See Conflicts of interest.
  • A partner who is paused or removed is told why and is heard.
  • Nobody at ATKAYVA may take money to admit a partner, to call one ahead of another or to overlook a failure. If anyone asks, tell the leadership.

Payments to partners

A network is held together by trust, and trust among working people is mostly a matter of being paid when promised. These are the principles we pay by.

2 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. Seven principles
  2. Tax
  3. If a payment is late
  4. If you disagree
  5. What nobody may ask of you
Partners
  • Partners overview

Join the network

  • Machinery owners
  • Transporters and fleet owners
  • Labour contractors
  • Consultants and suppliers

How it works

  • The standard
  • Payments
  • Register

Seven principles

  1. The rate is agreed before the work

    In writing. A message is enough. Rate, basis, hours, fuel, shifting and anything else that costs money.

  2. The work is counted together

    Hours on a log sheet. Trips and weights on slips. Attendance on a register. Each signed by your person and ours, shift by shift.

  3. The statement is yours to check

    At the end of the period we give you a statement of what we have counted. If your count differs, we compare records before the bill is raised.

  4. The bill is simple

    Your bill, in your name, with the period, the quantity, the rate and the tax that applies.

  5. Payment is on the date agreed

    The date is in your order. We do not wait to be asked.

  6. Payment is through the bank

    Into the account of the owner or the firm named in the order. Not in cash, and not to a third person.

  7. A deduction is explained

    In writing, with the reason and the record behind it. You may dispute it.

Tax

We deduct tax at source and deal with goods and services tax as the law requires, and we give you the certificates and statements you need for your own returns. If you are registered for GST, your invoice must carry your GSTIN and ours. We give ours with the work order.

If a payment is late

Tell the project manager. If it is not settled within two days, tell the leadership of the firm. The number is on the Contact page.

A labour contractor’s workers must be paid on time whether or not we have paid the contractor. So a late payment to a labour contractor is treated by us as an emergency.

If you disagree

  1. The supervisor

    For a difference in hours, trips or attendance. Usually settled from the signed sheets.

  2. The project manager

    For a difference in rate, a deduction or a claim.

  3. The leadership of the firm

    If you are still not satisfied. A partner will hear you in person.

What nobody may ask of you

Nobody at ATKAYVA may ask you for money, a gift, a discount or a favour in return for passing your bill, releasing your payment or giving you work.

If anyone does, do not pay. Tell the leadership. You will not lose work for it. You will keep it.

Careers

Work close to home, on jobs that matter, with a firm that pays what it promised. Fitters, welders, riggers, operators, drivers, supervisors and engineers are always wanted.

NKovaya

You do not have to leave this coast to build a trade. The plants are here. The work is here. What we look for is skill, steadiness and a person who does not hide a mistake.

There is no fee. Ever.

ATKAYVA never charges for a job, an interview, a medical, a uniform, a gate pass or a place on the register, and it does not use agents. If anyone asks you for money in our name, do not pay. See Fraud alert.

What to expect

  • A working day
  • Training and the ladder

We do not post vacancies with closing dates. Work on this coast comes in waves, and the register is always open. If your trade is here, apply.

Fitter and millwright
Assembles, aligns and repairs machinery. Reads a drawing, a level and a dial gauge. We look for ITI fitters and for people who learned beside a good one.
Welder
Joins steel so that it stays joined. Structural and pipe. We test every welder on a coupon. Qualifications in the 6G and 4G positions are valued.
Rigger
Slings and signals. The person who decides how a load leaves the ground and who stands where. We look for a cool head.
Mason
Brickwork, plaster, concrete finishing and repair.
Carpenter, shuttering
Builds the formwork that gives concrete its shape. Tight, true and strong.
Bar bender
Cuts, bends and fixes reinforcement to drawing, with the right cover.
Electrician
Site power, lighting and help to the plant’s electrical team. A licence or certificate as the law requires.
Painter and blaster
Surface preparation and coating to specification.
Helper
The hands every trade depends on. Where most tradesmen began.
Excavator operator
5 to 50 tonnes, with breaker. We look for someone who can feel the rock through the levers and who never swings over a person.
Crane operator
Pick-and-carry, mobile and crawler. Licensed, patient, and willing to refuse a lift that is not right.
Roller, mixer and pump operators
For earthwork and concrete.
Heavy vehicle driver
Tippers, trailers, low-loaders and bulkers. A valid licence, a clean record and good manners in a village.
Bus driver
Shift routes. Punctual to the minute and gentle on the brakes.
Car driver
For officers and visitors. Knows the roads from Diu to Bhavnagar.
Supervisor
Holds the drawing, the permit and the crew. Usually a tradesman who has earned it. Must be able to say no.
Site engineer, civil
Setting out, levels, reinforcement checks, pour planning, measurement and records. A diploma or degree.
Site engineer, mechanical
Erection, alignment, welding and lifting. A diploma or degree.
Safety officer
Inductions, permits, inspections and toolbox talks. Qualified in industrial safety. Reports to the leadership and not to the job.
Project manager
The single accountable face for a client. Plans, resources, decides and answers. Grown from within wherever possible.
Time office and wages
Attendance, wage sheets, provident fund and state insurance. Accuracy and fairness.
Accounts
Bills, payments, tax. Tally and patience.
Stores
Tools, consumables and material. Knows where everything is.
Transport coordinator
Vehicles, drivers, routes and trips. Lives on the telephone.
Mechanic
Keeps the network’s machines running. Diesel, hydraulics and field repairs.

What we look for in everyone

Whatever the role

Language

Our sites run in Gujarati and Hindi. English is useful for engineers and supervisors, who read drawings and write reports in it. Nobody is turned away for want of it.

Work with us

  • Roles
  • The call-up register
  • First jobs
  • Apply

What to expect

  • A working day
  • Training and the ladder
  • How we hire

What the register is

A list of people whose skill we have tested and whose fitness and background we have checked. They are not on our payroll through the year. They are called when there is work, paid for the work they do, and stood down when it ends.

Many work with us several times a year, shutdown after shutdown. Some have been on the register almost since it began.

Who it suits

  • A tradesman who wants work near home, and not a contract in another state
  • Someone with land or a family business who wants good wages for part of the year
  • A crew leader with a gang
  • A young person with a new certificate who needs a first site
  • An experienced hand who has had enough of travelling

How to join

  1. Apply

    On the work registration page, by telephone, or through a crew leader who already works with us.

  2. Show your trade

    A practical test. A welder welds. A fitter fits. A rigger slings and signals.

  3. Medical

    Arranged and paid for by us or by the contractor. A further check if you will work at height.

  4. Verification

    Identity, address and background, as plants require.

  5. Your name goes on

    With your trade, your grade and your village.

How a call comes

When a job is planned, the project manager lists the trades and numbers needed. Names are drawn from the register, starting with those who have worked well before and those who live nearest.

You are called or messaged, by us or by your crew leader, with the place, the dates, the shift and the wage. You say yes or no. A no does not count against you.

Before you start you are inducted at the plant and given your gate pass and protective equipment.

What you are paid, and when

The wage
The rate for your trade and grade, told to you before you start. Never less than the law requires.
Overtime
At the rate the law requires.
When
On the date you were told.
How
Into your own bank account wherever possible, with a record you can read.
Statutory cover
Provident fund, state insurance and employees’ compensation as the law provides.
Deductions
Only those the law permits. Nothing for the job, the pass or the helmet.

If any of this does not happen, go to the worker help desk.

What we expect

  • Come on the day, at the time
  • Follow the life-saving rules
  • Do the work properly
  • Tell the supervisor at once about an injury, a mistake or a danger
  • Treat everyone on site with respect

Moving up

The register is how we find our core team. A person who is skilled, safe and steady over several jobs is offered regular work when a place opens. See Training and the ladder.

There is no fee to join the register, and no one may take a cut of your wage for putting your name on it. See Fraud alert.

  • How we hire

If you hold an ITI certificate

Fitter, welder, electrician, mechanic diesel, turner or another trade. The certificate proves that you have been taught. A plant will teach you the rest.

Where you start
Beside an experienced tradesman, on real work, usually during a shutdown.
What you learn first
The plant. Its rules, its permits, its dangers and where everything is.
What you learn next
Your trade as it is practised: tolerances, sequence, and the hundred small things no classroom covers.
How you are judged
By the tradesman you work with and the supervisor above. On care, more than speed.

If you hold a diploma or a degree

Civil or mechanical. The polytechnic at Rajula and the engineering colleges of Saurashtra turn out good people every year, and most of them leave for the cities. You need not.

Where you start
As a trainee site engineer, under a site engineer who will make you take your own levels and check your own bars.
What you will do
Setting out, measurement, inspection requests, daily reports, pour planning. Records, a great many of them.
What you will learn
That the drawing and the ground do not always agree, and what to do when they do not.
Where it leads
Site engineer. Then, for those who can lead, project manager.

If you have no certificate

Most of the best tradesmen on this coast never had one. They began as helpers, watched, asked, and were given a tool when someone judged them ready.

Start as a helper. Come every day. Keep your eyes open. Ask the fitter why. Within a season your supervisor will know whether you have the hands for a trade, and which one.

What we ask of a beginner

Bring these, and we will supply the rest

What you can expect

  • A wage from the first day
  • Protective equipment, free
  • Induction and safety training before you touch anything
  • A tradesman who is responsible for you
  • No shouting for an honest mistake
  • A chance to move up. See Training and the ladder.

For women

Engineering, safety, stores, accounts and the time office are open to women as to men, and so is any trade a woman wishes to practise. See Respect at work for what we undertake.

For parents

Your son or daughter will work under a supervisor we trust, in a plant that enforces its rules, and will come home at night. If you would like to see where and with whom, ask. We will show you.

A working day

No two days on a site are the same, and all of them have the same shape. This is the shape, for anyone wondering what it is like.

3 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. At the gate
  2. The toolbox talk
  3. The permit
  4. The morning
  5. Tea
  6. Midday
  7. The afternoon
  8. Handing back
  9. Going home
  10. And at two in the morning
Careers
  • Careers overview

Work with us

  • Roles
  • The call-up register
  • First jobs
  • Apply

What to expect

  • A working day
  • Training and the ladder
  • How we hire

The bus leaves Rajula before the light. Half the seats are taken by people who have known each other since school. Somebody has brought thepla wrapped in newspaper. Nobody says much. Through the window the preheater tower is already visible, lit from top to bottom, with a plume going straight up in the still air.

At the gate

Passes are shown. Bags are checked. A new man is taken aside for his induction and will join after tea.

The night shift is coming out as the day shift goes in. A rigger going home tells a rigger going in what was left hanging on the crane. That exchange, thirty seconds long, is worth more than a page of handover notes, and a good supervisor makes sure it happens.

The toolbox talk

Ten minutes, standing in a half circle at the job, helmets on. The supervisor says what will be done today, in Gujarati and again in Hindi for the two welders from Uttar Pradesh. What can hurt us. What we have done about it. Who is new.

Then he asks whether anyone has seen anything. Someone always has. A grating that rocks. A cable lying in water. It is written down and one person is sent to deal with it.

The permit

The supervisor has already collected it. He reads out what it allows. The isolation is checked. Each man who will reach into the machine puts his own lock on.

Then the work begins.

The morning

This is when the heavy work is done, before the sun is high. A fitter and his helper strip a gearbox cover. Above them two welders are cutting out a worn chute plate, with a fire watch standing below holding an extinguisher and looking bored, which is how a fire watch should look.

The supervisor walks. He is not checking progress so much as watching hands and feet. Whose harness is hooked. Who is standing where a load will pass.

Tea

At ten the tea comes, sweet and strong, in a steel kettle. It is the one fixed point of the day in every plant in India. Jokes are made. The new man is teased gently and given the first cup.

Midday

Lunch is from a steel tiffin, in the shade. In May the hottest hours are for lighter work or none. The water pots are filled again. A man who has gone quiet is asked whether he feels well.

The afternoon

The plate is welded in. An inspector from the plant comes, looks, taps, nods and signs. The fitter closes the cover. Tools are counted back into the box, one by one, against the list. A spanner left inside a gearbox will find its way to the worst possible place.

Handing back

The area is swept. Scrap goes to the scrap bin. Locks come off, each by the man who put it on. The permit is signed off. The supervisor tells the control room that the equipment is theirs again.

Outside the gate the afternoon shift is coming in.

Going home

The bus is louder on the way back. Somebody’s daughter has passed an exam. Somebody’s brother is getting married after Diwali. The preheater tower slides past the window in the other direction.

By seven most of them are home.

And at two in the morning

Sometimes a telephone rings. A gate has jammed at the plant. The man who answers it puts on his boots. Nobody in the house asks where he is going. They have heard that ring before.

He will be at the gate in twenty minutes. That is the job.

This is a picture of an ordinary day, put together from many. The people in it stand for the people who do this work. None of them is a particular person.

Training and the ladder

Nobody is hired here to stay where they started. A helper who becomes a fitter is worth more to the next shutdown, and a fitter who becomes a supervisor is the person we will send to the next emergency.

2 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. The ladder
  2. How each step is earned
  3. What we teach
  4. Who teaches
  5. Certificates
  6. An honest word
Careers
  • Careers overview

Work with us

  • Roles
  • The call-up register
  • First jobs
  • Apply

What to expect

  • A working day
  • Training and the ladder
  • How we hire

The ladder

  1. Project manager

    The single accountable face for a client. Plans, resources, decides and answers.

  2. Site in-charge

    Runs a whole site, with several supervisors and trades.

  3. Supervisor

    Holds the drawing, the permit and the crew. Has the authority to stop a job.

  4. Crew leader

    A senior tradesman who leads a gang and teaches it.

  5. Tradesman

    Works to drawing without being watched. Fitter, welder, rigger, mason, operator.

  6. Semi-skilled

    Does part of a trade under a tradesman’s eye.

  7. Helper

    Fetches, carries, holds, cleans and watches.

You climb it from the bottom rung, and every rung is reached the same way: by doing the one below it well enough that someone trusts you with more.

How each step is earned

Helper to semi-skilled
A season or two of steady attendance, safe habits, and curiosity. Your tradesman says you are ready.
Semi-skilled to tradesman
A trade test. You do the job, to drawing, alone, and it is inspected.
Tradesman to crew leader
You have taught at least one person your trade, and you keep your gang safe.
Crew leader to supervisor
You can read drawings, write a report, manage a permit and say no to a client’s engineer politely.
Supervisor to site in-charge
You have run shutdown jobs and emergencies without drama.
Site in-charge to project manager
You can plan, price and answer for a whole job.

Engineers enter beside this ladder as trainees and are expected to spend their first years learning from the people on it.

What we teach

Safety
Induction for everyone. Work at height, confined space, lifting, hot work and isolation for those who do them. Refreshed regularly, and after any incident.
The plant
Each plant’s rules and layout, taught by people who know it.
The trade
On the job, beside someone better. Welders are given time and plate to practise for the next qualification.
A second trade
A fitter who can weld a little, a rigger who can signal a crane and drive a forklift: these people are never without work.
Reading and recording
Drawings, measurement, permits and the daily report, for those moving towards supervision.
First aid
For supervisors and for at least one person in every crew.

Who teaches

The people who do the work. Our best tradesmen are expected to teach, and are valued for it. A tradesman who guards his knowledge so as to stay indispensable has misunderstood how one becomes indispensable.

Certificates

Where a formal qualification exists and matters, such as a welder’s test, an operator’s licence or a safety qualification, we help people obtain it. We do not issue certificates of our own and call them qualifications.

An honest word

Not everyone climbs. Some excellent helpers have no wish to be anything else, and some fine tradesmen would be unhappy supervisors. There is respect and a living at every rung.

The six steps

  1. You apply

    On the page, by telephone, in person or through a crew leader.

  2. We talk

    A short conversation, usually on the telephone. Your trade, your experience, where you live, when you are free.

  3. You show your skill

    A practical test for trades and operators. A discussion and a site walk for engineers and supervisors.

  4. Medical examination

    At our cost. An additional examination for work at height.

  5. Verification

    Identity, age, address and background. Your original documents are looked at and returned to you.

  6. Offer and induction

    You are told your role, wage and start date plainly. Then induction: the plant’s hazards, the permit system and our code of conduct.

What we will never ask of you

  • Money, for anything
  • Your original certificates, to keep
  • Your bank PIN, a one-time password or a signed blank cheque
  • Work without pay “on trial”
  • A share of your first wage

If anyone asks for any of these in our name, do not agree. Call the number on the Contact page, or use the speak-up page.

How we choose

On skill, fitness, steadiness and character. Not on caste, religion, region or whose relative you are. A relative of someone in the firm is tested by someone who is not related. See Conflicts of interest.

Local people are preferred where skills are equal, because being near is itself a qualification for our kind of work.

Who cannot be hired

  • Anyone under eighteen
  • Anyone who fails the medical for the work in question. Other work may be possible.
  • Anyone who gives false documents

If you are not chosen

You will be told, and told why if we can say. For trades, your name can stay on our list for the next opening.
